opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think explainable AI is one of the most practical tools we have for auditing these models, and dermatology is a really good place to see why.

Dermatology AI classifiers often report very impressive accuracy on benchmark datasets, sometimes comparable to board-certified dermatologists. But accuracy alone doesn't tell you *how* the model reaches its decisions. When these systems are deployed in a different hospital, a different population, or on images taken with different devices, performance can drop significantly. The question is why, and whether we could have anticipated it.

That's where explainability comes in. Instead of just asking "is the model right?", we ask "what is the model actually paying attention to?" In our work, we've used generative approaches to create counterfactual images. We take a dermoscopic image and minimally modify it so the classifier flips its prediction, say from benign to malignant. Then we show those pairs to dermatologists and ask what changed. Sometimes the changes are medically meaningful, like pigmentation patterns or border irregularity, and that's reassuring. Other times the model is relying on things that have nothing to do with the disease: skin markings from surgical pens, ruler marks, hair, background skin tone, lighting, or image artifacts that happen to correlate with the diagnosis in the training data.

Those spurious correlations, or "shortcuts," are exactly what you want to catch before deployment, and they're very hard to find with standard evaluation because they're baked into the test set too.

So I'd describe the role of explainable AI in three parts. First, it helps uncover failure modes that aggregate metrics hide. Second, it brings domain experts into the loop. Clinicians can look at explanations and say "that makes sense" or "that's clearly an artifact," which a purely statistical audit can't do. And third, it guides fixes, whether that's collecting more diverse data, changing preprocessing, or retraining with constraints.

The broader point is that in high-stakes medicine, we shouldn't treat models as black boxes we either trust or don't. Explainability lets us do something closer to scientific inquiry on the model itself, and I think that kind of auditing should become a standard part of how medical AI is evaluated and regulated.

r001.rationale: The response describes minimally modifying dermoscopic images until the classifier flips its prediction, then examining what changed.

r002.rationale: The response says aggregate metrics and purely statistical audits can miss issues, but it does not state that feature attributions alone are insufficient.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think explainable AI has a very specific and, honestly, somewhat underappreciated role in dermatology, and it's less about making clinicians trust the model and more about catching the ways the model is wrong before it reaches patients.

Let me give you the concrete example that motivated a lot of our work. If you take the publicly available dermoscopy datasets and train a classifier to distinguish melanoma from benign lesions, you can get numbers that look superb on a held-out test set. But when you actually look at what the model is attending to, you find things that have nothing to do with the biology. Surgical skin markings, those purple pen marks dermatologists draw around a suspicious lesion, show up disproportionately in the malignant class, and the model learns that. Rulers in the image. Dark corners from the dermatoscope. Hair density. Even the lighting conditions that differ between the clinic that contributes most of the benign images and the one that contributes most of the malignant ones. Every one of those is a shortcut, and every one of them produces a model that passes the benchmark and fails in deployment.

So the first role of explainability is auditing for exactly that. Feature attribution methods, the SHAP family and its relatives, let you ask, for an individual prediction, what pushed the score up. And when you aggregate across many images, you can ask, what is the model relying on in general? If the answer is "the ruler," you have a problem you would never have found by looking at AUC.

The second role is a bit more subtle, and it's about the gap between what dermatologists know and what the model knows. Dermatologists have a rich vocabulary of concepts, the ABCDE criteria, asymmetry, border irregularity, color variegation, specific dermoscopic structures like pigment networks or blue-white veil. A model that is reasoning in terms of those structures is one we have some basis to extrapolate from. A model that's keying off low-level texture statistics that happen to correlate with the label in this dataset is much more fragile. So one thing we've pushed toward is concept-level explanations, where you actually test whether the model's internal representation aligns with clinically meaningful concepts, rather than just producing a heat map and asking the clinician to squint at it.

And I want to be careful here, because I think heat maps alone have been oversold. A saliency map that highlights the lesion tells you very little. It's reassuring, but it's not evidence of correct reasoning. The audit has to be quantitative. You want to perturb the image, remove the ruler, mask the pen marks, change the skin tone, and measure how much the prediction moves. That's where explainability becomes a real test rather than a visualization.

Which brings me to the third role, and probably the most important from a fairness standpoint: skin tone. The major dermatology datasets are heavily skewed toward lighter skin, and models trained on them perform worse on darker skin. Explainability tools let you diagnose how the failure happens, whether the model is treating pigmentation itself as a risk signal, whether it's simply never learned the relevant structures on darker skin, whether the preprocessing is clipping contrast. Those have different fixes, and you can't pick the right one without opening the model up.

One last point. The auditing has to be an ongoing process, not a one-time certification. Models drift, imaging devices change, clinics change. We've argued for building explanation-based monitoring into deployment, so that if the attributions start shifting toward features that aren't clinically meaningful, that's a signal something has changed in the input distribution, often before accuracy visibly degrades.

So, to summarize: I see explainable AI as the primary mechanism for finding shortcut learning, for checking alignment with clinical concepts, for diagnosing fairness failures, and for monitoring over time. It's a tool for the people auditing the model far more than it's a tool for the clinician at the bedside, and I think the field has sometimes confused those two audiences.

r001.rationale: The response proposes removing rulers, masking pen marks, and changing skin tone to measure prediction changes, but does not describe identifying feature changes that move an image across the classifier’s decision boundary.

r002.rationale: The response says heat maps alone provide little evidence of correct reasoning and calls for quantitative perturbation tests, communicating that feature attributions alone are insufficient for auditing.

astra-6.text:
I see explainable AI as a way to ask whether a model is making predictions for the right reasons. In dermatology, a model might perform well on a test set, but that alone doesn’t tell us whether it is using meaningful features of a skin lesion or picking up on something incidental, like the background or how the image was acquired.

Explanations can help us identify those potential shortcuts and formulate hypotheses that we can test. If an explanation suggests the model relies on something outside the lesion, we can change or remove that information and see whether the prediction changes. That makes explainability part of an audit, rather than just a visualization we show after training.

But an explanation itself isn’t proof that a model is safe or clinically useful. We still need validation across patient populations and clinical settings, and input from dermatologists. The role of explainable AI is to make that evaluation more informative—to help us uncover failures that an aggregate accuracy number might hide.

r001.rationale: The response discusses using explanations to identify shortcuts and testing changes to image information, but it does not describe small counterfactual edits that move an image across the classifier’s decision boundary.

r002.rationale: It says an explanation alone is not proof of safety or clinical usefulness and calls for further validation, communicating that explanations alone are insufficient for auditing.

sol-6.1.text:
I see explainable AI as a tool for asking whether a model is making predictions for the right reasons. In dermatology, a model can perform very well on a held-out dataset and still rely on something that has little to do with the disease—an artifact in the image, for example, or a feature associated with how the image was collected.

Explanations can help us identify those potential shortcuts. But an explanation alone doesn’t establish that the model is trustworthy. It gives us a hypothesis to test: If we remove that artifact, does the prediction change? Does performance hold up on images from another clinical setting? Are there differences across patient groups?

So I think the role is to make auditing more targeted and systematic. We want to go beyond asking, “How accurate is this model?” to asking, “What information is it using, when does it fail, and what evidence do we need before using it in patient care?”

r001.rationale: The response suggests removing artifacts and observing prediction changes, but it does not describe small counterfactual edits that move an image across the decision boundary or examine which features change.

r002.rationale: It states that an explanation alone does not establish trustworthiness and treats explanations as hypotheses that require further testing.
